metaDescription: Six electric snow blowers under $500, battery and corded, compared on clearing width, throw distance and runtime so you can pick the right one.
expertTake: The Greenworks 80V 20-inch is the strongest battery machine under the $500 cap, and the Westinghouse WSnow22 is the best corded value if your driveway sits near an outlet. The DEKOPRO is the cheapest way to get a real rubber-tipped auger thrower. Skip this price band entirely if your driveway is long, sloped or regularly buried under more than 8 inches of wet snow, because only a two-stage gas machine handles that.
introParagraphs: Under $500 you are shopping for single-stage electric snow throwers. They use a rubber-edged auger that scrapes the pavement and flings the snow out of a chute in one motion, which makes them light, quiet and simple to store.

The trade is capability. These machines suit paved driveways, walks and decks with light to moderate snowfall. Prices move and the $500 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated, so confirm before you buy.

products.name: Greenworks 80V 20-Inch Brushless Snow Blower
products.description:
The Greenworks runs on the maker's 80V platform, which means each amp-hour carries far more energy than a 40V pack of the same rating. Its brushless motor drives a 20-inch auger housing, and the design goal is steady throughput rather than a headline wattage number. In this price band that makes it the machine most likely to finish a two-car driveway on a single outing.

The tradeoff is that the listing ships with one 4Ah battery and a fast charger. The WORX WG461 in this guide ships with two 6Ah-class packs, so you get longer total runtime from that machine if you will not buy a second Greenworks pack. Single-stage design also means the auger touches pavement, so it belongs on smooth asphalt or concrete, not gravel.

Ownership is simple. There is no oil, spark plug or carburetor, and the brushless motor has no brushes to wear. Plan on a second 80V pack if you also own other Greenworks 80V tools, because the platform is shared and the pack is the expensive part. Store the pack indoors, since cold garages cut its output before you even start.
products.bestFor: Homeowners with a paved two-car driveway who want the most capable battery machine under the cap.
pros: 80V platform stores more energy per pack than 40V
Brushless motor needs no brush replacement
20-inch path cuts passes on a wide driveway
No fuel, oil or carburetor upkeep
cons: Only one 4Ah battery in the listing
Single-stage auger is no match for deep wet snow

products.name: WORX WG461 40V 20-Inch Cordless Snow Blower
products.description:
WORX builds this machine around two 20V PowerShare packs that combine to make 40V. Each is a 6Ah pack, so you have 12Ah of capacity to spend before swapping, and the 20-inch by 10-inch intake is among the biggest openings you will see at this price. The maker quotes a throw of up to 35 feet, which is a best-case figure with light powder.

That makes it the better pick than the Greenworks if total runtime matters more than platform power. The Greenworks has a stronger 80V system but only one 4Ah pack, while the WORX has two larger packs in the box. Those packs also work in the maker's other 20V tools, which lowers the cost of entry if you already own that ecosystem.

Expect to carry two packs in and out of the cold, and to charge them one after the other. The 10-inch intake is a limit, not a promise: when snow is deeper than the housing you should take it in two passes, top layer first.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want long battery runtime out of the box and already use 20V WORX tools.
pros: Two 6Ah packs included for long total runtime
20 by 10 inch intake clears wide passes
Packs fit other 20V PowerShare tools
Brushless motor is low maintenance
cons: 40V system has less punch than 80V rivals
Stated 35 ft throw needs dry powder
Two packs take time to recharge

products.name: IONMAX 48V 18-Inch Cordless Blower by Snow Joe
products.description:
Snow Joe pairs two 24V IONMAX packs for 48V output and a 1200W brushless motor. The quoted rate of 700 pounds of snow per minute is a maximum under ideal conditions, so treat it as a ceiling rather than an average. At 18 inches wide it is slightly narrower than the 20-inch Greenworks and WORX, which means more passes on a wide driveway.

Its selling point is balance. It is lighter and easier to turn than the 20-inch machines, and the 10-inch intake still takes a normal storm in two lifts. If you have a short driveway and a long walkway, the narrower body is easier to steer around planters and steps.

The dual-pack system means you must keep both batteries charged and warm. The maker positions it for light to moderate snow, and that is an honest limit: wet heavy snow will slow the auger and drain the packs faster than the label suggests.
products.bestFor: Smaller driveways and walkways where light handling matters more than maximum width.
pros: 1200W brushless motor with solid torque
Easier to maneuver than 20-inch rivals
Dual 24V packs share the IONMAX platform
10-inch intake handles normal storms

products.name: Westinghouse WSnow22 22-Inch Corded Snow Blower
products.description:
The WSnow22 swaps the battery for a 15 amp cord, and that single change gives it unlimited runtime and the widest 22-inch path in this guide. A rubber-tipped steel auger throws snow out to roughly 25 feet, with a stated rate of 840 pounds per minute. Dual LED lights help with pre-dawn clearing.

Its limits are the cord and the reach. You need an outdoor-rated extension cord of suitable gauge and a power point near the area, so a long driveway is awkward. Compared with the DEKOPRO, it is wider by four inches and moves a few more pounds per minute, which matters on a walk-and-deck job but not a huge amount.

Cord handling is the whole ownership story. Keep the cord behind you, never run over it with the auger, and store it dry. There is no battery to cold-soak or fuel to stabilize, which makes this the lowest-hassle machine here.
products.bestFor: Short driveways, decks and walks near an outdoor outlet.
pros: Unlimited runtime with no battery to charge
22-inch path is the widest here
LED lights help in the dark
No batteries or fuel to maintain
cons: Cord limits reach and can be run over
Needs a heavy-gauge outdoor extension cord
Single-stage auger struggles on deep snow

products.name: DEKOPRO 18-Inch 15A Corded Snow Blower
products.description:
The DEKOPRO is the cheapest machine in this guide that still carries a rubber-edged steel auger and a proper chute. A two-blade auger opens an 18-inch by 9-inch path, and the chute rotates through 180 degrees so you can aim the throw away from the car. Its 15 amp motor is quoted at 800 pounds per minute.

It gives up two inches of width and an inch of intake depth to the Westinghouse, so it fits shorter jobs. If your driveway is two cars wide you will make more passes than with the 22-inch Westinghouse. The brand is also less established, which affects parts and support, so inspect the auger and paddles on arrival.

Because there is no battery, the machine sits in the garage all summer with no upkeep beyond a wipe and a look at the cord. That simplicity is the point of buying it.
products.bestFor: A tight budget and a short, paved area close to an outlet.
pros: Lowest cost way into a real auger thrower
180-degree chute aims snow cleanly
No battery or fuel to maintain
Compact size stores easily
cons: 18 by 9 inch intake needs extra passes
Cord restricts how far you can work

products.name: Wild Badger Power 40V 20-Inch Cordless Blower
products.description:
Wild Badger ships this 20-inch machine with two 4Ah 40V batteries and a fast charger, so you can run one pack while the other charges. The intake is 10 inches tall and the maker quotes a throw of up to 26 feet. That is a shorter throw than the 35 feet the WORX claims, which matters when you want to clear snow beyond a flowerbed.

Against the WORX it carries smaller packs but a larger voltage rating, so total energy is in the same ballpark as the WORX rather than clearly better. Its edge is simply that everything comes in one box. The brand is newer, so check the warranty terms before you commit.

Keep both packs indoors until needed, and avoid using the machine after a pack has been sitting in a freezing garage. That one habit does more for runtime than any spec on the label.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a complete two-battery kit with no ecosystem lock-in.
pros: Two batteries and charger in the box
20-inch path clears quickly
Brushless motor reduces upkeep
Hot-swapping avoids a long wait
cons: 26 ft throw is shorter than the WORX
Newer brand with a thin track record
4Ah packs run down on wet snow

buyingCriteria.explanation: Every machine here is single-stage: a rubber-tipped auger that touches the ground and throws snow itself. That works to roughly 8 inches of snow on paved surfaces and fails on gravel, because it flings stones. If your driveway is long or your storms regularly top a foot, no machine in this guide is the right tool. Check the intake: the Greenworks 80V and the WORX both list 10 inches at most.

Voltage alone does not decide power. Multiply volts by amp-hours to compare stored energy, so the WORX at 40V and two 6Ah packs holds more usable energy than a single 4Ah 80V Greenworks pack in the same time frame. Platform quality matters too: 80V motors can pull harder under load. A mistake buyers make is comparing a bare tool listing to a two-battery kit.

Corded machines such as the Westinghouse WSnow22 at 15A and the DEKOPRO give unlimited runtime for a fraction of the battery machine's weight and cost. The cost is a cord that tangles and an outlet requirement. A good rule is to stay corded only if the farthest point you must clear is within about 100 feet of an outdoor outlet, using the right cord gauge.

Width times intake height tells you how many passes a storm needs. The Westinghouse at 22 inches is widest, the Snow Joe at 18 inches by 10 inches is slimmer. Wider is faster but heavier to turn at the end of each row. If you have a narrow walk, a 18-inch unit is easier to handle than the wide ones.

Lithium packs lose output sharply near 0 F. Keep packs indoors and insert them just before use. The two-pack kits from WORX and Wild Badger let you swap a warm pack in mid-job. Buying a single-pack kit and storing it in an unheated garage is the most common reason a machine seems underpowered in January.

Throw distance claims such as 35 ft on the WORX or 26 ft on the Wild Badger are for light powder in ideal conditions, and wet snow throws a fraction of that. A chute that rotates freely, like the 180-degree one on the DEKOPRO, lets you change direction without stopping. Check wind direction before you set the chute, because throwing into a headwind wastes time.

specDecoder.meaning: The width of the cut path per pass. A wider path reduces the number of passes but adds weight and a bigger turning radius.

specDecoder.meaning: The tallest snow the housing can swallow in one pass. Deeper snow must be taken in layers or the auger will bog.
specDecoder.watchFor: Most 40V machines here list 10 inches, while the DEKOPRO lists 9 inches.

specDecoder.meaning: A 15 amp motor draws the maximum a standard household circuit supports. That sets how much snow the motor can handle without tripping.

howWeEvaluated.title: Intake and path size
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the listed clearing width and intake height for each machine. Fewer passes per storm is a real time saving. The Westinghouse at 22 inches sets the top end of this lineup.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power source
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated battery machines from corded ones and weighed what each trade costs in practice. Cords limit reach, batteries limit runtime. The Wild Badger and WORX packs show how the battery kits compare.

howWeEvaluated.title: Auger design
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the auger material and whether it is rubber-tipped. A rubber edge protects the pavement and the housing. The Westinghouse specifically lists a steel auger with rubber tips.

howWeEvaluated.title: Real ownership upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged what each machine asks of you after year one. Batteries must be stored properly, cords must be coiled and inspected. All six machines avoid fuel and oil upkeep.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value at the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for features per listing price band: brushless motors, included batteries and lights. The Greenworks 80V and WORX two-pack kit represent the high end of this group.

cards.label: Battery
cards.text: The Greenworks 80V, WORX WG461, Snow Joe IONMAX and Wild Badger give you freedom and no cord to tangle. Runtime is limited and packs must be kept warm. They cost more per unit of capability.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: The Westinghouse WSnow22 and DEKOPRO run as long as the power stays on. They are light and need no charging, but the cord limits where you can work and must be handled with care.

howToChoose.note: Pick battery if your area is far from an outlet; pick corded if the whole job is within cord reach.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A path of 20 inches or more and an intake near 10 inches, plus enough battery capacity to finish without a mid-job recharge.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Greenworks 80V and WORX WG461 both clear 20 inches. The WORX has more packs, the Greenworks has more power per pack. The Westinghouse is wider at 22 inches but tied to a cord.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want to cut passes and runtime anxiety. The Greenworks 80V and WORX WG461 reduce both. Also spend up if you already own the maker's other tools and can share batteries.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your area is small and near an outlet. The DEKOPRO or Westinghouse WSnow22 does the same job as the battery machines for less. Save on the Snow Joe if you only need a single pass.

maintenance.why: Rubber tips wear down, and a worn edge stops clearing to the pavement. Replace it when the rubber is flush with the metal.
Cold cuts output and shortens lifespan. Keep them at partial charge in a cool, dry place.
A nick can expose a live wire. Replace damaged cords before they cause a shock.
Wet snow left in the housing freezes and jams the auger. Dry it before storing.
Vibration loosens bolts on the housing and chute. Tighten them to avoid a rattle or breakage.

faq.q: Are electric snow blowers worth it under $500?
faq.a: For paved driveways and walks with light to moderate snow, yes. They are quiet, need no fuel and start instantly. They do not replace a two-stage gas machine for deep or heavy snow.

faq.q: How much snow can these handle?
faq.a: Most listings give a 9 or 10 inch intake and suit snow up to about 8 inches. Take deeper snow in layers, and expect poor results with wet, heavy or packed snow.

faq.q: Battery or corded, which is better?
faq.a: Battery is better for freedom of movement and longer reach. Corded is better for unlimited runtime and lower price. Choose based on how far the work is from an outlet.

faq.q: Will a bigger voltage always last longer?
faq.a: No. Runtime depends on voltage multiplied by amp-hours and on the motor efficiency. A 40V machine with two 6Ah packs can outlast an 80V machine with one 4Ah pack.

faq.q: Can I use these on a gravel driveway?
faq.a: Not safely. Single-stage augers contact the surface and throw stones. Use a two-stage machine with adjustable skid shoes for gravel.

faq.q: How long should one of these last?
faq.a: The motor and housing are simple and should last many winters. The battery is the wear item, usually a few hundred cycles, so protect it from cold and overcharging.
